title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a BST
directAnswer: Exploit the BST ordering: start at the root and walk down. If both `p` and `q` are greater than the current node, the LCA is in the right subtree; if both are smaller, go left; the moment they split (one on each side, or one equals the current node) the current node IS the lowest common ancestor. O(h) time, O(1) space iteratively — no need for the generic O(n) tree-LCA search.

remember.formula:
node = root
while node:
    if p.val < node.val and q.val < node.val: node = node.left
    elif p.val > node.val and q.val > node.val: node = node.right
    else: return node   # split or match → LCA
rules: Use the **BST ordering** — don't fall back to the generic O(n) LCA search you'd use on a plain binary tree.
The LCA is the **first node where p and q diverge** (one ≤ node ≤ other), including the case where node equals p or q.
Both-greater → go **right**; both-smaller → go **left**; anything else → **return node**.
Iterate with O(1) space — the recursion is tail-recursive, so a `while` loop is strictly better.
The problem guarantees both nodes **exist** in the tree, so you never walk off the end before finding the answer.
whenToUse: Finding the LCA in a **binary search tree** specifically (values are ordered)
You can compare target values against the current node to pick a direction
You want O(h) rather than O(n) and don't need to handle arbitrary binary trees
Ancestor / range / 'where do two paths from the root diverge?' questions on a BST
antiSignals: Tree is a **plain binary tree** (no ordering) → use the recursive return-up LCA (LeetCode 236)
Nodes might **not exist** in the tree → you must verify presence, not just split
You need the LCA of more than two nodes or a forest → different formulation
It's a general graph, not a tree → use binary lifting / Tarjan's offline LCA
remember.takeaway: On a BST, the LCA is simply the split point: the first node from the root that sits between `p` and `q` in value. Comparing against the node's value to choose a direction turns an O(n) tree walk into an O(h) descent — the same 'let the ordering guide you' idea behind Validate BST and Kth Smallest in a BST.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you recognize that the BST invariant lets you prune to a single root-to-node path instead of searching the whole tree — and whether you can express the descent in O(1) space.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Writing the generic O(n) binary-tree LCA (recursing both subtrees) and ignoring the BST ordering entirely, or getting the comparison directions backwards so you walk away from the answer.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: Name the split-point insight out loud, do it iteratively in O(1) space, and contrast it with the LeetCode 236 plain-tree version to show you know exactly which property you're exploiting.

problemStatement:
Given a binary search tree (BST), find the lowest common ancestor (LCA) of two given nodes `p` and `q` in the BST.

The lowest common ancestor is defined between two nodes `p` and `q` as the lowest node in the tree that has both `p` and `q` as descendants (where we allow ***a node to be a descendant of itself***).

Both `p` and `q` exist in the BST and all node values are unique.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10⁵]
p ≠ q, and both p and q exist in the BST
understanding: We're walking down a sorted tree looking for the point where the paths to `p` and `q` part ways. Because every node's left subtree holds smaller values and its right subtree holds larger ones, comparing values tells us which way each target lies. A node is the LCA exactly when `p` and `q` are no longer on the same side of it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree guaranteed to be a valid BST?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes — that's the whole point. The ordering invariant is what lets us pick a direction by comparing values instead of searching both subtrees.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are p and q guaranteed to be present in the tree?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. Because both exist, the descent always reaches a valid split point — we never need to verify existence separately.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can a node be an ancestor of itself?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. If p is an ancestor of q (or p == the split node), then p itself is the LCA. The 'else' branch covers node == p or node == q.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Are the values unique?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, so comparing `p.val`/`q.val` against `node.val` is unambiguous — there's never a tie to break.

examples.explanation: 2 is in the left subtree of 6 and 8 is in the right subtree, so they split at the root — 6 is the LCA.
4 lives in the subtree rooted at 2, so 2 is an ancestor of itself and of 4 — the LCA is 2.
1 is the left child of 2; 2 is its own ancestor, so the LCA is 2.

approaches.name: Generic Tree LCA — Recurse Both Subtrees
approaches.whenToMention: Mention it as the fallback that works on any binary tree, then point out it ignores the BST ordering and is therefore slower than necessary.
hints: Forget the ordering for a second: on a plain binary tree, how would you know whether a subtree contains p, q, or both?
Recurse into left and right. If p and q come back from different sides, the current node is the LCA.
If both come back from the same side, the LCA is deeper on that side; if neither side has them, return null up the chain.
approaches.complexityReasoning: In the worst case we visit every node once (we don't use the ordering to prune), so O(n) time; the recursion stack is as deep as the tree, O(h).
approaches.explanation:
This is the universal LCA algorithm — it works on *any* binary tree, ordered or not. It searches the tree bottom-up and lets each node report whether `p` or `q` was found beneath it.

**The reporting contract.** Each recursive call returns a non-null node if it found `p`, `q`, or an LCA somewhere below. At a node, we recurse left and right. If *both* sides return non-null, then `p` and `q` were found on opposite sides, so the current node is their lowest common ancestor. If only one side returns non-null, we pass that result upward — the LCA (or the only target seen so far) lives on that side.

**Why it's wasteful on a BST.** Nothing here uses the fact that left < node < right. We blindly explore both children of every node we touch, so in the worst case the whole tree is visited. On a *sorted* tree we can do far better by using a single comparison to discard an entire subtree at each step.

**Why mention it anyway.** It's the correct answer to the sibling problem (LeetCode 236, plain binary tree), and saying 'here's the general method, but the BST lets me prune' demonstrates you understand exactly which property you're exploiting.
approaches.insight: The generic method finds the LCA by detecting the node where the two targets first appear on *different sides*. That's the same 'split point' idea as the optimal solution — the BST version just uses value comparisons to find the split in O(h) instead of exploring everything in O(n).

dryRun.intro: Each call reports whether p or q was found below it; the node that hears 'yes' from both sides is the LCA.

steps.action: recurse left (subtree of 2) and right (subtree of 8)

code.python:
# Definition for a binary tree node.
# class TreeNode:
#     def __init__(self, x):
#         self.val = x
#         self.left = None
#         self.right = None
def lowestCommonAncestor(self, root: 'TreeNode', p: 'TreeNode', q: 'TreeNode') -> 'TreeNode':
    if root is None or root is p or root is q:
        return root
    left = self.lowestCommonAncestor(root.left, p, q)
    right = self.lowestCommonAncestor(root.right, p, q)
    if left and right:
        return root
    return left if left else right

java.explanation: Base case: an empty subtree returns null; hitting p or q reports that target upward.
Both targets found on opposite sides → this node is the split point, i.e. the LCA.
Otherwise propagate whichever side found something (or null if neither did).

python.line: if root is None or root is p or root is q:
python.explanation: Empty subtree returns None; reaching p or q bubbles that node up.
Found on both sides → current node is the lowest common ancestor.

python.line: return left if left else right
python.explanation: Pass the non-null side upward; None if neither side held a target.

pitfalls: Using this on a BST and never exploiting the ordering — correct but O(n) instead of O(h).
Forgetting the `root == p || root == q` base case, which handles 'a node is its own ancestor'.
Recursing only one side based on a guess — without the BST ordering you must check both.

approaches.name: BST Descent — Walk to the Split Point (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for a BST. Frame it as 'use the ordering to pick a direction, stop at the split'.
hints: You're on a sorted tree. If both p and q are larger than the current node, where can they possibly be?
If both targets are greater than node.val, go right; if both are smaller, go left. What does it mean when they're on opposite sides?
The first node where p and q are NOT both on the same side is their LCA — that includes the case where node equals p or q. Loop until you hit it.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each step moves one level down the tree and does O(1) comparison work, so the cost is the height h (O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate). Iterating uses no extra stack → O(1) space.
approaches.explanation:
On a BST we never need to look at both children. The ordering tells us which single direction can contain both targets, so we descend a single root-to-node path until the targets diverge.

**The split-point insight.** Pick any node on the path from the root. If `p` and `q` are *both* greater than it, both live in its right subtree, so the LCA must be further right. If both are *smaller*, both live left. The only remaining case is that one target is ≤ node ≤ the other (or one of them equals the node). At that node, the paths to `p` and `q` go down different children — this is the lowest node that still has both as descendants, i.e. the LCA. We can stop the instant we reach it.

**Why this is O(h), not O(n).** Each comparison lets us discard an entire subtree, so we touch one node per level and never branch. That collapses the search from 'visit everything' to 'follow one path', exactly like an ordinary BST search for a value.

**Why iterative beats recursive here.** The recursion is tail-recursive — the recursive call is the last thing each frame does — so it carries no useful stack information. Rewriting it as a `while` loop reuses a single pointer variable and brings space down from O(h) to O(1). State that trade explicitly; it's the kind of detail interviewers reward.

**Why we never run off the tree.** The problem guarantees both `p` and `q` exist, so a split point always lies on the shared prefix of their two root-paths. We are guaranteed to return before `node` becomes null.
approaches.insight: The LCA on a BST is the unique node whose value lies between `p.val` and `q.val` inclusive, and is closest to the root among such nodes — equivalently, the first node where the two search paths diverge. Recognising 'LCA = first divergence of two BST searches' is the entire trick.

pitfalls: Flipping the comparison directions so you walk away from the targets.
Using strict `>`/`<` but forgetting the equality case lands in the else branch (which is exactly what handles node == p or node == q).
Recursing instead of looping — correct, but wastes O(h) stack for a tail-recursive walk.

commonMistakes: Using the generic O(n) both-subtrees recursion and ignoring the BST ordering entirely.
Getting the comparison directions backwards, so the pointer moves away from p and q.
Assuming you must handle the case where p or q is missing — the problem guarantees both exist.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Ignoring the BST ordering
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Recursing into both subtrees works but is O(n). On a BST a single comparison discards half the tree, giving O(h). Interviewers expect you to use the property you were handed.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the equality (self-ancestor) case
commonMistakesDetailed.why: If you only branch on strict greater/less and treat 'node equals a target' as a separate special case, you complicate the code. Letting equality fall through to the else branch returns the node correctly — a node is its own ancestor.

patternNote: BST-guided descent. Whenever the tree is ordered, compare the target(s) against the current node to discard a whole subtree per step, turning an O(n) tree walk into an O(h) path. Same family as Search in a BST, Validate BST, and Kth Smallest in a BST.
